Download image Share… Facebook Text message WhatsApp Copy link Link to these numbers Prices: electricity = Residential average, January–August 2026 (August 2026 YTD) (EIA Table 5.6.B). Natural gas = Residential average of monthly prices, November 2025–March 2026 (last heating season) (EIA). Heating oil and propane = EIA weekly residential price, week of 2026-10-19; states EIA doesn't survey use the regional or U.S. price. Climate = NOAA heating degree days. You can type your own prices. The short answer If you heat with oil or propane, a heat pump usually costs less to run. If you heat with natural gas, it often costs about the same or more, unless your electricity is cheap. If you heat with electric baseboards, a heat pump almost always costs less. Why? Heating oil costs about $6.19 a gallon in the U.S. this month (EIA, week of 2026-10-19). EIA expects homes that heat with oil to spend about $2,115 this winter (Nov–Mar), up 21%. Homes on natural gas: about $640, down 9% (EIA Winter Fuels Outlook). Example homes (2,000 sq ft, average insulation, HSPF2 8.5) HomeNow, per yearHeat pump, per yearHeat pump costs Massachusetts, heating oil$2,610$1,936$674 less Pennsylvania, propane$1,753$1,260$493 less Ohio, natural gas$607$1,119$512 more These are running costs only. Your real numbers depend on your home, your system and the weather. See how it works. Popular comparisons Heating oil vs heat pumpPropane vs heat pump Natural gas vs heat pumpElectric baseboard vs heat pump Prices and savings in all 50 states + DCIs there still a heat pump tax credit? (No: 25C ended) Words on this page Heat pump: an electric system that moves heat from outside air into your home. It also cools in summer. COP: how many units of heat you get for each unit of electricity. COP 2.5 means 2.5 times more heat than a space heater on the same power. HSPF2: a heat pump's heating rating over a season. Higher is better. HSPF2 ÷ 3.412 ≈ average COP in a mild climate. Btu: a unit of heat. One gallon of heating oil holds about 138,500 Btu (EIA).Questions people askDoes a heat pump save money over oil?Usually yes. At $6.19 a gallon (EIA U.S. average, week of 2026-10-19), oil heat costs much more per unit of heat than a heat pump in most states. Check your state's electricity price in the calculator.Does a heat pump save money over natural gas?Often not by much. Gas is cheap in many states this winter. A heat pump can still win where electricity is cheap or where you'd also replace an air conditioner.Do heat pumps work in cold climates?Yes, but they make less heat and use more power when it is very cold. Cold-climate models keep working below 0°F. Our calculator lowers the efficiency for colder states.Is there still a federal tax credit for heat pumps?No. The 25C credit (30%, up to $2,000) does not apply to equipment placed in service after December 31, 2025, per the IRS. Some state and utility rebates still exist.SourcesEIA Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.6.B: residential electricity price by state, year to dateEIA: Natural gas prices by state (residential, monthly)EIA Heating Oil and Propane Update (weekly residential prices)EIA Winter Fuels Outlook, October 2026EIA: British thermal units (Btu) and fuel heat contentNOAA NCEI Climate at a Glance / nClimDiv statewide degree daysNext stepSee what rebates are left in 2026 &rarr;The 25C tax credit ended. Here is what you can still get.

## Heat Pump vs Oil, Propane and Gas in Alabama (2026 Prices)
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/state/alabama/

Short answer for Alabama: at this winter's prices, a heat pump costs less to run than heating oil, propane and electric baseboard in a typical 2,000 sq ft home. Electricity here averages 16.51¢ per kWh, 9% below the U.S. average of 18.19¢ (#29 cheapest of 51). Alabama heating prices this winter FuelPriceCost per million Btu of heatSource Electricity16.51¢/kWh$18.50 with a heat pump (COP 2.62); $48.39 with baseboardsEIA, Jan–Aug 2026 average Heating oil$6.19/gal$53.85 (83% efficient)EIA weekly, 2026-10-19, U.S. average price (EIA has no weekly price for this state) Propane$3.57/gal$43.41 (90% efficient)EIA weekly, 2026-10-19, state price Natural gas$1.67/therm ($17.32/Mcf)$18.58 (90% efficient)EIA, Nov 2025–Mar 2026 average Yearly cost: your fuel vs a heat pump For a 2,000 sq ft home with average insulation in Alabama's warm climate (2,669 heating degree days a year), with a heat pump rated HSPF2 8.5 (we use COP 2.62 here): Heating nowNow, per yearHeat pump, per yearHeat pump costsBreak-even power priceHeating oil$1,150$395$755 less$0.481Propane$927$395$532 less$0.387Natural gas$397$395$2 less$0.166Electric baseboard$1,033$395$638 less$0.432 Cheapest to run today in this example: a heat pump. Break-even means: if you pay less than this per kWh, the heat pump is cheaper than that fuel. Download image Share… Facebook Text message WhatsApp Copy link Link to these numbers Rebates in Alabama The federal 25C tax credit for heat pumps ended for equipment placed in service after Dec 31, 2025 (IRS). Federal Home Energy Rebates (HEAR/HOMES) are run by each state, and many states have not opened. Since Sept 1, 2026, new HEAR rebates can't pay to replace oil, propane or gas heat unless the old system stays in place (DOE Program Notice 26-2). Check your state energy office and your electric utility. Full 2026 rebate guide. The break-even electricity price is $0.166 per kWh.What is the most common way to heat a home in Alabama?Electricity (this includes homes that already have a heat pump): 64% of homes use it as their main heating fuel, per EIA's 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey.What does electricity cost in Alabama?16.51 cents per kWh on average for homes, January–August 2026 (EIA Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.6.B). ## Heat Pump vs Oil, Propane and Gas in Colorado (2026 Prices)
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/state/colorado/

## Heat Pump vs Oil, Propane and Gas in Hawaii (2026 Prices)
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/state/hawaii/

Short answer for Hawaii: Hawaii has a warm climate, so most homes need very little heating. Heating costs are small whichever system you use; a heat pump matters more here for cooling. Electricity here averages 46.41¢ per kWh, 155% above the U.S. average of 18.19¢ (#51 cheapest of 51). ## Heating Oil vs Heat Pump 2026: Cost Calculator by State
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/heating-oil-vs-heat-pump/

Heating oil costs about $6.19 a gallon in the U.S. (EIA, week of 2026-10-19). EIA expects oil-heated homes to spend about $2,115 this winter, 21% more than last winter. In most states a heat pump costs less to run than an oil furnace or boiler. One gallon of oil gives about 138,500 Btu of heat, and an 83% efficient boiler delivers about 115,000 Btu. To make the same heat, a heat pump with a COP of 2.5 uses about 13.5 kWh. So if your electricity costs less than $0.46 per kWh, the heat pump wins. In Massachusetts, our example home would spend $2,610 on oil and $1,936 with a heat pump. Many oil homes keep the boiler as a backup for the coldest days. That is allowed under the new federal HEAR rules (see rebates). ## Propane vs Heat Pump 2026: Which Costs Less to Heat Your Home?
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/propane-vs-heat-pump/

Propane averages $2.69 a gallon in the U.S. (EIA, week of 2026-10-19), but prices vary a lot: from about $1.65 in North Dakota to about $4.93 in Florida (state prices EIA surveys). Where propane is costly, a heat pump usually wins. In the Midwest, where propane is cheap, it can be close. One gallon of propane holds about 91,452 Btu (EIA). A 90% furnace delivers about 82,000 Btu. A heat pump with COP 2.5 makes that with about 9.6 kWh. So the heat pump wins if your power costs less than about $0.28 per kWh at the U.S. average propane price. ## Natural Gas vs Heat Pump 2026: Running Cost by State
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/natural-gas-vs-heat-pump/

Natural gas is the cheapest heat in most states this winter. EIA expects gas-heated homes to spend about $640 this winter, 9% less than last winter. A heat pump beats gas mainly where electricity is cheap or gas is costly. A therm of gas is 100,000 Btu. A 90% furnace delivers 90,000 Btu. A heat pump with COP 2.5 uses about 10.6 kWh to make that heat. So at $1.50 a therm, the heat pump wins only if power costs under about $0.14 per kWh. Many people still choose a heat pump to replace an old air conditioner, since it cools too. ## Electric Baseboard vs Heat Pump: How Much Can You Save? (2026)
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/electric-baseboard-vs-heat-pump/

A heat pump uses about 50–70% less electricity than baseboard heat for the same warmth, because it moves heat instead of making it. Baseboards have a COP of 1. A heat pump with COP 2.5 uses 60% less. This is the switch that still qualifies for federal HEAR rebates after Sept 1, 2026: replacing electric equipment with more efficient electric equipment (DOE Program Notice 26-2), where your state has opened its program. ## Heat Pump Rebates 2026: What's Left After the 25C Tax Credit Ended
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/heat-pump-rebates-2026/

Short answer: the federal 30% heat pump tax credit (25C, up to $2,000 a year) is gone for equipment placed in service after Dec 31, 2025. Federal Home Energy Rebates still exist in some states, but since Sept 1, 2026 they can't pay to replace oil, propane or gas heat with a heat pump unless you keep the old system. State and utility rebates are separate and may still help. What changed ProgramStatus in 2026Source 25C Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit (heat pumps: 30%, up to $2,000/yr)No credit for property placed in service after Dec 31, 2025IRS FAQ 25D Residential Clean Energy Credit (geothermal heat pumps, solar)No credit for expenses made after Dec 31, 2025IRS FAQ HEAR / HEEHR (electric appliance rebates, up to $14,000 per home)Run by states; only in some states. New reservations since Sept 1, 2026: no fuel switching; electric-to-electric upgrades and new construction allowed; may need insulation and air sealing firstDOE Notice 26-2, DOE HOMES (whole-home savings rebates, up to $8,000)Run by states; rules vary by stateDOE Utility and state programsSeparate from federal rules. Many still offer heat pump rebatesYour utility / state energy office If you heat with oil, propane or gas Under DOE's new guidance, a HEAR rebate can still help with a heat pump if the existing fossil-fuel system stays in place and is not taken out. The heat pump no longer has to be your main heat (NASEO FAQ, Sept 2026). Rebates reserved on or before Aug 31, 2026 follow the old rules. If you heat with electric baseboards or an old heat pumpThis is the main case HEAR covers now: replacing electric equipment with more efficient electric equipment. How to check what you can getCheck your state energy office page for HEAR/HOMES status (the ENERGY STAR HEAR page lists state programs). Check your electric utility's rebate page. These are often the biggest rebates left. Ask installers which rebates they process. Get the rebate amount in writing before you sign. Use our payback calculator with the quote and rebate. Watch out: some ads still promise a "30% federal tax credit" on heat pumps. That credit doesn't apply to systems installed in 2026. Questions people askIs there a federal tax credit for heat pumps in 2026?No. The IRS says the 25C credit does not apply to property placed in service after December 31, 2025.Can I get a HEAR rebate to replace my oil furnace with a heat pump?Not for new reservations since Sept 1, 2026, unless the oil system stays in place. Rules come from DOE Program Notice 26-2; your state runs the program.What is the biggest heat pump rebate left?It depends on where you live. Check your electric utility and your state energy office first.SourcesIRS: FAQs on changes to 25C, 25D and other credits under the One Big Beautiful Bill (P.L. 119-21)IRS: Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit (25C)U.S. Department of Energy: Home Energy Rebates programDOE Home Energy Rebates Program Notice 26-2 (HEAR/HEEHR changes)NASEO: Home Energy Rebates FAQ, September 2026ENERGY STAR: State and Tribal rebate programs (HEAR)Next stepWork out your payback &rarr;Put in your quote and rebates. ## Heat Pump Tax Credit 2026: Did 25C End? (Yes — Here's What Remains)
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/heat-pump-tax-credit-2026/

Yes, it ended. The 2025 tax law (Public Law 119-21) ended the 25C Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit for property placed in service after December 31, 2025 (IRS). What it was25C gave 30% of the cost of a qualifying heat pump, up to $2,000 a year. It applied to heat pumps placed in service from 2023 through 2025. Who can still claim itIf your heat pump was placed in service in 2025, you claim it on your 2025 tax return using IRS Form 5695. A system installed in 2026 doesn't qualify. What's leftState and utility rebates, and federal HEAR/HOMES rebates in states that run them. See the 2026 rebate guide.Questions people askCan I claim 25C for a heat pump installed in January 2026?No. The IRS says no credit is allowed for property placed in service after December 31, 2025.I paid in 2025 but it was installed in 2026. Do I qualify?25C depends on when the property is placed in service. Check the IRS FAQ and a tax professional.SourcesIRS: FAQs on changes to 25C, 25D and other credits under the One Big Beautiful Bill (P.L. 119-21)IRS: Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit (25C)Next stepSee rebates that still exist &rarr;State, utility and DOE rebates in one place.

## Heat Pump Payback Calculator: How Long Until It Pays for Itself?
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/heat-pump-cost/

A heat pump costs money up front. This tells you how many years of lower bills it takes to pay that back. Get your yearly savings from the savings calculator first. Installed price from your quote ($) Rebates you will get ($)Yearly savings ($) Simple payback The starting numbers are examples only. Use your own quote. The yearly savings start at our Massachusetts oil example ($674). Things that change the answerReplacing an air conditioner too? A heat pump also cools, so compare against the cost of a new AC plus a new furnace, not zero. Rebates: utility rebates can be large. Get them in writing.Fuel prices: oil prices change a lot from year to year (EIA).Insulation: sealing air leaks first lowers the size and cost of the system. Questions people askHow much does a heat pump cost?It varies by home size, ducts, brand and region. Get at least three written quotes. We don't publish price averages we can't verify.What is a good payback time?Shorter is better. Many people also count comfort, summer cooling and replacing old equipment, not just the payback years.SourcesEIA Winter Fuels Outlook, October 2026U.S. Department of Energy: Home Energy Rebates programENERGY STAR: Air-source heat pumpsNext stepCheck what size you need &rarr;A rough size so you can compare quotes.

## Mini Split Size Calculator: What Size Heat Pump Do I Need?
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/mini-split-size-calculator/

This gives a rough size to help you compare quotes. A good installer should do a room-by-room load calculation (called Manual J) before you buy. Area to heat (sq ft) InsulationGoodAverageDrafty Coldest normal winter temperature (°F) Heat needed on the coldest days How we estimate itWe use the same heat-loss assumption as our savings calculator (3, 4 or 5.5 Btu per sq ft per degree day for good, average or drafty homes). Heat loss per hour = that number × area ÷ 24 × (65°F − outdoor temperature). It's a planning number, not a design. Why the cold-temperature number mattersHeat pumps make less heat when it's colder. Check how much heat a model makes at 5°F on the NEEP cold-climate list or its spec sheet, not just its name ("12k", "18k"). Questions people askHow many square feet does a 12,000 Btu mini split heat?It depends on insulation and climate. In our average-insulation example at 5°F outdoors, 12,000 Btu/hr covers about 1,200 sq ft. Drafty homes need more.Is a bigger heat pump better?No. Too big can short-cycle and feel less comfortable. Size it to your home's heat loss.SourcesNEEP: Cold-climate air-source heat pump product listENERGY STAR: Ductless heating and cooling (mini-splits)AHRI Directory of certified product performanceNext stepFind rebates before you buy &rarr;Check your state and utility before you sign.

## Portable and Window Heat Pumps: Running Cost vs a Space Heater
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/portable-heat-pump/

A space heater turns 1 kWh of power into 3,412 Btu of heat (COP 1). A small window or portable heat pump can make 2 or more times that much heat from the same power, when it isn't too cold outside. Heater (making 5,000 Btu/hr)Power usedCost per hour at 29.3¢/kWh (NY avg) Space heater (COP 1)1.47 kW$0.43 Window/portable heat pump (COP 2)0.73 kW$0.21 Window/portable heat pump (COP 2.5)0.59 kW$0.17 Things to knowPortable units with one hose can pull cold air into the room, which lowers real savings.Window heat pumps are popular for apartments where you can't install a mini-split. Look for the heating capacity at low temperatures on the spec sheet.During a power outage, no electric heater works without backup power. See Ready.gov. Questions people askIs a window heat pump cheaper than a space heater?Yes, when it's working as a heat pump. At COP 2 it uses about half the electricity for the same heat.SourcesEIA Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.6.B: residential electricity price by state, year to dateEIA: British thermal units (Btu) and fuel heat contentENERGY STAR: Air-source heat pumpsReady.gov: Power outagesNext stepRun your own numbers &rarr;Pick your state and fuel. ## HSPF2 to COP Converter (and What a Good HSPF2 Is)
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/hspf2-to-cop/

HSPF2 ratingAverage seasonal COP The math: HSPF2 is Btu of heat per watt-hour of electricity over a test season. One watt-hour = 3.412 Btu. So COP ≈ HSPF2 ÷ 3.412. An HSPF2 of 8.5 ≈ COP 2.49. The HSPF2 test season represents a moderate climate. In colder states, real COP is lower. Our calculator lowers it by 10% for states with 5,000–7,000 heating degree days and 20% above 7,000. This is our planning assumption, not a test result. Compare real models on the AHRI directory and the NEEP cold-climate list.SourcesAHRI Directory of certified product performanceNEEP: Cold-climate air-source heat pump product listENERGY STAR: Air-source heat pumpsEIA: British thermal units (Btu) and fuel heat contentNext stepRun your own numbers &rarr;Pick your state and fuel. It takes 30 seconds.

## How the Heat Pump Savings Calculator Works
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/methodology/

The steps Heat your home needs per year. Home-size mode: square feet × your state's heating degree days × 3, 4 or 5.5 Btu (good, average, drafty insulation). Usage mode: last winter's fuel × its heat content × your system's efficiency. Cost now: heat needed ÷ (fuel heat content × efficiency) × price. Heat pump cost: heat needed ÷ 3,412 Btu/kWh ÷ COP × electricity price. COP: the COP you enter, or HSPF2 ÷ 3.412, adjusted for climate: ×1.05 below 3,000 heating degree days, ×1.0 for 3,000–5,000, ×0.9 for 5,000–7,000, ×0.8 above 7,000. Fixed numbersHeating oil138,500 Btu/gal (EIA)Propane91,452 Btu/gal (EIA)Natural gas100,000 Btu/therm; 1,036 Btu per cubic foot, so 1 Mcf ≈ 10.36 therms (EIA)Electricity3,412 Btu/kWh (EIA) Default efficiencyOil 83%, propane and gas 90%, electric resistance 100% (you can change these) PricesPrices: electricity = Residential average, January–August 2026 (August 2026 YTD) (EIA Table 5.6.B). Natural gas = Residential average of monthly prices, November 2025–March 2026 (last heating season) (EIA). Heating oil and propane = EIA weekly residential price, week of 2026-10-19; states EIA doesn't survey use the regional or U.S. price. Climate = NOAA heating degree days. You can type your own prices.Why these periods? Electricity uses the newest year-to-date average so it includes winter months. Gas uses last winter's months because summer gas prices per unit are much higher and don't reflect heating bills. Oil and propane use EIA's newest weekly survey, which runs October through March. Our assumptions (not official numbers)The heat-loss factors and the climate adjustment for COP are our own planning assumptions, chosen to give typical results. They are not from a government source. Usage mode, with your real fuel use, is more accurate. LimitsRunning costs only. No purchase, install, maintenance or demand charges.Doesn't model backup heat strips, dual-fuel or time-of-use rates.State averages hide big local differences. Use your own bill prices when you can.SourcesEIA Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.6.B: residential electricity price by state, year to dateEIA: Natural gas prices by state (residential, monthly)EIA Heating Oil and Propane Update (weekly residential prices)EIA Winter Fuels Outlook, October 2026EIA: British thermal units (Btu) and fuel heat contentNOAA NCEI Climate at a Glance / nClimDiv statewide degree daysNOAA U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020Next stepRun your own numbers &rarr;Pick your state and fuel. It takes 30 seconds.

## About Heat Pump Savings Check
URL: https://j6-cloude.github.io/heat-pump-savings/about/

Heat Pump Savings Check is a free, independent calculator that helps people see if a heat pump would lower their heating bill. It uses public data from the EIA, NOAA, the IRS and the U.S. Department of Energy. Independent free tool. Not affiliated with any government agency, utility or heat pump manufacturer.
